The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then always returns `false` in both branches (if enabled, return false; otherwise fall through to return false). This means the function is dead/confusing code that always disables SQL expressions no matter the feature flag state. While the net effect (always disabled) achieves the security goal of this PR, the logic is misleading and buggy — if someone later tries to re-enable the feature by flipping the flag, it will silently not work, and the variable `enabled` is unused in a meaningful way. This should be simplified to `return false` directly with a comment, to avoid confusion and dead code since the flag check is a no-op.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TablesList still calls RunCommands which always errors

TablesList() calls duckDB.RunCommands(...) against the new stub DB in db.go, which unconditionally returns `errors.New("not implemented")`. Combined with reader.go's always-false enable check, SQL expressions are effectively disabled, but this leaves two different disablement mechanisms (feature flag always false, and stub DB always erroring) that could get out of sync if one is fixed without the other, potentially creating confusing behavior or partial re-enablement bugs in the future.

false_positives.candidate:
No test coverage asserting SQL expressions are disabled

The PR's stated purpose is to disable SQL expressions to prevent an RCE/LFI vulnerability, but no test was added to pkg/expr (e.g., in reader_test.go or sql_command_test.go) that verifies QueryTypeSQL requests are rejected with the expected error, or that NewSQLCommand/Execute paths fail safely when the feature is toggled on. Given the security-critical nature of this change, a regression test ensuring the vulnerability can't be silently reintroduced is important and currently missing.

The stub methods in db.go (TablesList, RunCommands, QueryFramesInto) take parameters that are never used in the function bodies. While harmless at runtime, this can trigger unused-parameter lint warnings and signals that this is dead placeholder code; a comment explaining the stub's purpose (and that it intentionally disables SQL expressions) would help future maintainers understand why DB does nothing instead of assuming it's an incomplete implementation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocking search index build now in NewResourceServer constructor can cause long startup / deadlock risk

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously, which triggers searchSupport.init() that builds the full index for all namespaces before returning from the constructor. For large installations this can take a very long time, blocking server startup (and anything that constructs ResourceServer, e.g. module server wiring, tests, or other services that expect fast construction). Any caller relying on fast/non-blocking construction (previously relying on lazy init during the first gRPC call) will now be blocked indefinitely or until index build completes, with no timeout or context deadline applied to the Init call.

NewResourceServer now returns error on index build failure, changing behavior/contract for existing callers

Previously, failures in search index initialization (e.g., transient DB/network issues during index build) only affected the first gRPC call lazily. Now any error returned from s.search.init(ctx) during NewResourceServer causes construction of the ResourceServer to fail entirely, preventing the whole module/server from starting. This is a notable behavior change: any transient issue in index building (e.g., one misbehaving namespace or stats collection failure) will block the entire resource server from being created, with no partial-start fallback.

Stop() sets s.initErr directly outside of the sync.Once guarded path used by Init(). If Init() is still running concurrently (e.g., background watcher goroutine) while Stop() executes, there's a race writing/reading s.initErr without synchronization (no mutex, no atomic). This was already present before, but now that Init() runs synchronously at construction and the once can still fire later from other paths, the race window remains and reviewers should flag that initErr access is unguarded.

totalBatchesIndexed increment and errgroup closure captures loop variable info unsafely in older style

In the init loop, group.Go closures use the loop variable `info` from `for _, info := range stats`. Depending on Go version semantics (pre-1.22) and since the closures run concurrently, capturing `info` without taking a local copy inside the goroutine can lead to data races/incorrect namespace reported if Go version < 1.22. Also totalBatchesIndexed++ is incremented from multiple goroutines without synchronization (concurrent writes to the same int from errgroup goroutines), which is a data race since initWorkers can run several goroutines in parallel.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Changing RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE breaks documented/established exit code contract

Any external scripts or CI/CD pipelines built against the previous exit code mapping (4 = recreate required) will now behave incorrectly, interpreting 'feature disabled' as 'recreate needed' or vice versa. Since this tool is explicitly documented for scripting purposes, exit code changes are a backward-incompatible break and should be called out prominently in release notes, not silently remapped during a preview-stage PR.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource.getId() names inconsistent with resource naming scheme (V1)

In V1 GroupPermissions, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() strips the 'group.resource.' prefix off resource.getName() to produce a group id, consistent with getGroupResourceName(). This is fine for V1, but GroupPermissionsV2 (new file) instead adds groupResource.getId() (the resource's internal ID, not the group ID) to the granted set in its getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(). Since resources for V2 groups are created/named by group ID directly (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returning group.getId() as resource name), using resource.getId() instead of resource.getName() will return wrong values (internal resource UUIDs instead of actual group IDs), breaking downstream usages like UsersResource.searchForUser() and getUsersCount() that expect group IDs to filter users by UserModel.GROUPS attribute.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

canQuery no longer grants fallback for group-scoped view access

canQuery() now is `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_USERS) || canView()`, but canView() only returns true for global view/manage roles or hasPermission at the Users resource level; it does not account for per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions. Previously an admin who can only view users of specific groups (via requireQuery in UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource) might have been allowed to query based on group-scoped access, and is now blocked. This changes the admin's ability to list/search users they otherwise have group-scoped visibility into - search endpoints call requireQuery() before falling back to group-restricted search, so such admins would get a 403 instead of a filtered result set.

englishFile is computed by regex-replacing the locale suffix in the current file's absolute path, assuming the English file lives in the exact same directory with the same basename structure. For files under resources-community vs resources, and across different theme categories (account/login/admin/email), this heuristic may not reliably resolve to the actual English source file if directory layouts differ, silently falling back to empty string on exception, masking real validation issues since englishValue becomes "" and HTML in translations would then be verified against the strict POLICY_NO_HTML even when the English source legitimately contains HTML.

false_positives.candidate:
Member routes for add/remove not scoped to a specific group id

The new routes `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` are declared inside `resources :groups do ... end` as collection-level routes (not `member do ... end`), producing paths like `/admin/groups/members` instead of `/admin/groups/:group_id/members`. The controller actions rely on `params.require(:group_id)` passed in the body/query instead of the URL, which works but is inconsistent with REST conventions used elsewhere in this file (e.g., `/users/:username/groups/:group_id`), and means the group id is not validated as part of the route, making CSRF-style/method confusion or missing-param errors less obvious. This is a design inconsistency rather than a crash, but it diverges from the rest of the routes file and could confuse future API consumers expecting `/admin/groups/:id/members`.

members endpoint always issues two queries, no caching, breaking automatic/large group handling

The previous implementation had special-case handling for automatic groups (limiting/offsetting large automatic groups to avoid timeouts/truncation issues) with a TODO about more than 200 groups truncating. The rewritten `members` action removes that special case and always does `group.users.count` plus a paginated query for every group type with a default limit of 50. For very large automatic groups (e.g. trust_level groups with tens of thousands of members) this now always executes a full COUNT(*) on every request, which can be an expensive query under load, especially since this is a public user-facing endpoint (`GroupsController`), not admin-only. There's no caching of the total count, which was presumably one of the reasons the former code treated automatic groups specially.

addMembers never clears the input field after adding, acknowledged by stale TODO

The `addMembers` action contains a TODO: "should clear the input" but it's left unaddressed. After adding members, the `usernames` property is not reset, so the user-selector field keeps showing the previously entered usernames, which is confusing when the admin wants to add another batch of members.

members iterated in group.hbs but never defined for the new group (create) flow

The template references `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` and `user_count`, which are populated only after `model.findMembers()` succeeds (triggered from the route). For a new group (no `id` yet), `{{#if id}}` guards the whole members+add-members block so this is fine, but once a group is saved for the first time via `create()`, `members`/`user_count`/`offset`/`limit` are never populated (findMembers is only called from the route's `setupController`, not after `create()`). This means immediately after creating a group and transitioning to `showGroup`, the newly created group's member section will render with stale/undefined pagination data until the admin navigates away and back, since `admin_group_route.js`'s `model` hook just looks up the already-cached group object rather than re-fetching it with members.

This can be used to probe internal network resources if embeddable_host's server redirects to internal IPs. No protection against redirects to non-http(s) schemes or internal addresses is implemented.

Although `apiDeletes` is later awaited via Promise.all, the push itself happens asynchronously after forEach has already returned, so there's a window where `apiDeletes` may not yet contain all the deletion promises before the outer code proceeds to use the array (e.g., `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`), risking some deletions being missed from the final await.
